title: Why James McAvoy's Wanted Deserves Another Look
excerpt:
The 2008 action film Wanted paired James McAvoy with Angelina Jolie and Morgan Freeman.
A retrospective argues that its inventive action and remarkable cast deserve renewed attention.
body_md:
James McAvoy is closely associated with Professor Charles Xavier in the X-Men franchise, but his comic-book movie career had an important earlier chapter. Wanted, released in 2008, gave the actor an opportunity to lead an extravagant action film before his superhero fame became firmly established.

McAvoy plays Wesley Allan Gibson, an ordinary young man drawn into a clandestine organization known as the Fraternity. Angelina Jolie portrays Fox, a member who helps guide him into this dangerous world. The film became particularly memorable for its stylized gunfights and the spectacular idea of bullets bending through the air.

Wanted is a loose adaptation of a comic-book miniseries rather than a faithful scene-by-scene recreation. The original material places greater emphasis on recognizable superhero and supervillain conventions, while the film introduces substantial ideas of its own. The famous bullet-curving technique, for example, was not a defining feature of the original comic.

The movie earned more than $340 million worldwide, helping McAvoy demonstrate his range beyond work such as Atonement, The Chronicles of Narnia and the British series Shameless. A recent retrospective argues that the performance helped audiences recognize him as a viable action lead. That is an assessment of his career trajectory, not proof that the role directly secured his later casting as Professor X.

Its ensemble remains another major attraction. Morgan Freeman plays Sloan, a senior figure in the Fraternity. Common appears as a weapons instructor, while Terence Stamp portrays Pekwarsky. Chris Pratt also has a small role from the period before his breakthrough on Parks and Recreation and his later Marvel success.

Wanted fits into a broader pattern of McAvoy taking on heightened genre material. He subsequently starred in X-Men films and appeared in Split and Glass, which reinterpret superhero conventions, while Atomic Blonde was adapted from a graphic novel. Each project uses a different blend of action, character work and comic-book influence.

A sequel to Wanted was discussed but never materialized. The current article is a retrospective appreciation rather than a new production announcement. Its case for revisiting the film rests on the energetic direction, distinctive visual ideas, strong box-office performance and unusually impressive cast.
